content.text:
I've built the frontend as an Expo app with HeroUI Native and Uniwind, running on mock data. It's running now at **http://localhost:8081** (also `npm run web`). I tested the main flows in the browser at iPhone size, and typecheck and lint pass. I couldn't run it on iOS: Xcode's license hasn't been accepted (`sudo xcodebuild -license`), so the native tab bar and Liquid Glass parts haven't been run yet.

**Screens**
- **Chat:**
  - Answers stream in, with a collapsible thinking section.
  - Your messages are solid blue bubbles; assistant replies are text on black.
  - The message box has glass styling. Next to it are a model picker, a Thinking control (Auto, Off, or whatever levels that model supports), a Deep Research toggle, photo attach (with a warning if the model can't read images), hold-to-talk with a waveform, and send/stop.
  - Every reply ends with a sources bar (sources list, read aloud, share, save, regenerate, copy).
- **History:** search, grouped by date, open or delete chats. It starts with 5 sample chats.
- **Memory:** an on/off switch, category filters, edit/add/delete, and export as JSON.
- **Settings:** add or edit providers (ID, URL, key, headers, fetch models). Each model shows what it supports, with "Run probes" and tap-to-override. There are also custom instructions and settings for sub-agents, web access, search, voice and the probe spend cap.

**Inline UI components:** all 16 from the PRD catalog, plus a location prompt and a "save to memory?" card. Each one is checked against its schema before it shows, displays a placeholder while loading, and sends your taps back to the model.

**Try these starter prompts:**
- **Movies near me:** allow location, then showtimes and a map that stay in sync; pick a time and the assistant follows up.
- **Savings chart:** drag the slider and the chart recalculates; drag across the chart to read values.
- **Sub-agents:** approve the plan, watch the workers run live (one partly fails on purpose), then get a comparison.
- **Research:** answer the clarifying question, edit the plan, watch progress, then get a cited report.
- Weather, packing list, booking form, headphones, timeline and setup steps each show their own component. "Remember that I'm vegetarian" saves to memory with an undo.

**Things to know**
- **Web is only a test setup.** HeroUI doesn't officially support web, so on web the glass is a blur and the tab bar is a custom one. On iOS the system tab bar and Liquid Glass are used instead.
- **Workarounds for web bugs:** I added three:
  - `metro.config.js` fixes a startup crash on web caused by Uniwind.
  - `global.css` sets fixed hover colours because HeroUI's colour helper can't read them on web.
  - Buttons inside chat cards no longer use HeroUI's `isDisabled`, which fired a press the user never made on web.
- **The map is a drawn stand-in** so it works offline; MapLibre comes with the native build. Posters and site icons are also generated, not real images.
- **Fonts:** I downloaded Satoshi and Moderniz into `assets/fonts`. Moderniz's readme says it's free for commercial use, which answers the PRD's open licence question. It's an all-caps typeface, so titles appear in capitals.

**For the backend later:** all the fake answers come from one place, `runAssistant` in `src/lib/store.ts`. Swap that for the Convex stream; the message format stays the same, so the screens won't need changes. The README lists everything to try and how the code is laid out.

ui.content:
The bottom tabs are gone; navigation is now a left side menu that works like your reference. The chat fills the screen with the input box at the bottom. I tested it in the browser at iPhone size, and typecheck and lint pass.

**How it works**
- **Opening and closing:** the button at the top left opens the menu, and so does swiping in from the left edge. The chat slides right as a rounded card, like in the reference. Tap or swipe the chat to close it; Escape also works on web.
- **Menu contents, top to bottom:**
  - "Atlas" with a search button, which opens History with the search box ready to type.
  - History and Memory.
  - Recents: your 6 latest chats. The open one is highlighted, and a blue dot marks a chat that's still replying.
  - "View all", which goes to History.
  - At the bottom, the settings icon on the left and a white "New chat" button on the right.
- **History, Memory and Settings** now open as full pages with a back button. Opening a chat from History takes you straight back to it.

**Two changes you might not expect**
- **The menu button shows three lines, not three dots.** I used the lines icon from your reference. If you'd rather keep the dots, it's a small swap in `ChatHeader.tsx`.
- **Chat options moved to the title.** The three dots used to open incognito, rename and delete. Now you tap the chat title at the top, which has a small arrow next to it.

**Fix along the way:** custom text colours on some labels (the "New chat" label, selected chips) were being overridden by the default white, so the "New chat" label didn't show. `Text.tsx` now lets your own colours win.

The new menu code is in `src/components/navigation/SideDrawer.tsx` and `NavPanel.tsx`. The pages moved out of the `(tabs)` folder into `src/app/`, and I deleted the old tab files. One line in the README still mentions "native tabs" (the `npm run ios` comment) and needs updating.

content.text:
The bottom tabs are gone; navigation is now a left side menu that works like your reference. The chat fills the screen with the input box at the bottom. I tested it in the browser at iPhone size, and typecheck and lint pass.

**How it works**
- **Opening and closing:** the button at the top left opens the menu, and so does swiping in from the left edge. The chat slides right as a rounded card, like in the reference. Tap or swipe the chat to close it; Escape also works on web.
- **Menu contents, top to bottom:**
  - "Atlas" with a search button, which opens History with the search box ready to type.
  - History and Memory.
  - Recents: your 6 latest chats. The open one is highlighted, and a blue dot marks a chat that's still replying.
  - "View all", which goes to History.
  - At the bottom, the settings icon on the left and a white "New chat" button on the right.
- **History, Memory and Settings** now open as full pages with a back button. Opening a chat from History takes you straight back to it.

**Two changes you might not expect**
- **The menu button shows three lines, not three dots.** I used the lines icon from your reference. If you'd rather keep the dots, it's a small swap in `ChatHeader.tsx`.
- **Chat options moved to the title.** The three dots used to open incognito, rename and delete. Now you tap the chat title at the top, which has a small arrow next to it.

**Fix along the way:** custom text colours on some labels (the "New chat" label, selected chips) were being overridden by the default white, so the "New chat" label didn't show. `Text.tsx` now lets your own colours win.

The new menu code is in `src/components/navigation/SideDrawer.tsx` and `NavPanel.tsx`. The pages moved out of the `(tabs)` folder into `src/app/`, and I deleted the old tab files. One line in the README still mentions "native tabs" (the `npm run ios` comment) and needs updating.

ui.content:
I've added animations as you move through the app. Most of them respond to something you do, and all of them are skipped when the phone's Reduce Motion setting is on. I checked them in the browser at iPhone size, and typecheck and lint pass. I haven't run any of it on an iPhone yet.

**Side menu**
- The menu's three lines fold into an X as the menu opens. This follows your finger during a swipe rather than running on a timer.
- Menu items slide in one after another, also tied to the drag: a slow swipe reveals them slowly, a quick flick snaps them in.
- When a chat moves to the top of Recents, the list re-sorts smoothly instead of jumping (iPhone only, not on web).

**History, Memory and Settings pages**
- Each section rises in, one after the other, when the page opens.
- As you scroll, the big title fades out and a small title appears in a top bar, like iOS apps do. Pulling down past the top stretches the big title slightly.
- Deleting a chat, searching, or filtering memories fades rows in and out, and the remaining rows slide into place (iPhone only).
- The selection highlight in the option switches in Settings now slides to the new choice instead of jumping.

**Chat**
- Switching chats fades the conversation in. Messages already in a chat appear instantly; only new ones animate.
- Your message rises up from the input box, and replies fade in.
- The mic, send and stop buttons swap with a small pop. Photo attachments pop in and out.
- If you scroll up through a long chat, a "jump to latest" button appears above the input box.
- The empty chat screen reveals its suggested prompts one by one. The chat title fades when you switch chats.
- When a reply finishes, its sources icons pop in one at a time, and the arrow on "Thought for…" turns when you open it.

**Every tappable thing** now shrinks and dims slightly under your finger and springs back when you let go. Small buttons and full-width rows feel equally deep.

**Things to know**
- **Web shows simpler versions.** The animation library only handles its basic animations properly on web. The springier versions and the "slide into place" effects made sections stack on top of each other there, so on web they fall back to plain fades and slides.
- **Smaller fixes:** the switch labels were getting cut off ("Free …"), so I reduced their padding. The row of icons under each reply overflowed on smaller phones, so it now shows 3 source icons instead of 4.

All the timings live in one file, `src/lib/motion.ts`, so you can tune the feel in one place.

content.text:
I've added animations as you move through the app. Most of them respond to something you do, and all of them are skipped when the phone's Reduce Motion setting is on. I checked them in the browser at iPhone size, and typecheck and lint pass. I haven't run any of it on an iPhone yet.

**Side menu**
- The menu's three lines fold into an X as the menu opens. This follows your finger during a swipe rather than running on a timer.
- Menu items slide in one after another, also tied to the drag: a slow swipe reveals them slowly, a quick flick snaps them in.
- When a chat moves to the top of Recents, the list re-sorts smoothly instead of jumping (iPhone only, not on web).

**History, Memory and Settings pages**
- Each section rises in, one after the other, when the page opens.
- As you scroll, the big title fades out and a small title appears in a top bar, like iOS apps do. Pulling down past the top stretches the big title slightly.
- Deleting a chat, searching, or filtering memories fades rows in and out, and the remaining rows slide into place (iPhone only).
- The selection highlight in the option switches in Settings now slides to the new choice instead of jumping.

**Chat**
- Switching chats fades the conversation in. Messages already in a chat appear instantly; only new ones animate.
- Your message rises up from the input box, and replies fade in.
- The mic, send and stop buttons swap with a small pop. Photo attachments pop in and out.
- If you scroll up through a long chat, a "jump to latest" button appears above the input box.
- The empty chat screen reveals its suggested prompts one by one. The chat title fades when you switch chats.
- When a reply finishes, its sources icons pop in one at a time, and the arrow on "Thought for…" turns when you open it.

**Every tappable thing** now shrinks and dims slightly under your finger and springs back when you let go. Small buttons and full-width rows feel equally deep.

**Things to know**
- **Web shows simpler versions.** The animation library only handles its basic animations properly on web. The springier versions and the "slide into place" effects made sections stack on top of each other there, so on web they fall back to plain fades and slides.
- **Smaller fixes:** the switch labels were getting cut off ("Free …"), so I reduced their padding. The row of icons under each reply overflowed on smaller phones, so it now shows 3 source icons instead of 4.

All the timings live in one file, `src/lib/motion.ts`, so you can tune the feel in one place.

<skill name="frontend-design">
---
name: frontend-design
description: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
license: Complete terms in LICENSE.txt
---

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

</skill>

<skill name="empryo">
---
name: empryo
description: Configure Empryo (settings, models, providers, MCP servers, Cells) and answer questions about it.
version: 19
digest: 92e6d8a9f373e360681764642c72e6e086371d2f0891e346a2e95407baa969de
---

# Empryo

Empryo is an AI coding agent. It builds a map of the user's repository (the Genome), edits code by symbol, works with many model providers, and runs in three places: a desktop app, a terminal UI and a headless CLI.

Your training data is out of date for this product. Empryo ships often, and config keys, slot names, provider ids and flags change between releases. Look up the docs before you answer.

## Retrieve

Use the documentation MCP server when it is connected. It is a Streamable HTTP server at `https://empryo.com/mcp`, read-only, with no sign-in. If the user has not connected it, that is the URL they add. Its tools are prefixed with the server name they configured (commonly `empryo-docs`):

| Tool | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `search_docs` | Find the right page and anchor. Start here. |
| `read_docs` | Read one page, or one exact section via `anchor`. |
| `list_docs` | Enumerate pages, or the sections of one page. |
| `current_release` | The published version and its artifacts. |

Search first, then read the exact section the results name. Read a whole page only when the answer really needs all of it. An empty `anchor` selects the introduction; leaving `anchor` out returns the full page.

Without MCP, fetch over HTTP:

- `https://empryo.com/api/docs/search?q=<terms>&scope=docs`, ranked sections with exact selectors
- `https://empryo.com/docs/<slug>.md`, one page as Markdown (`.txt` for plain text)
- `https://empryo.com/docs/<slug>.exports.json`, that page's per-section Markdown and text URLs
- `https://empryo.com/llms.txt`, the index, `llms-full.txt` is the whole corpus in one request

A URL fragment does not limit an HTTP response. To retrieve one section, fetch its own export URL from `.exports.json`.

## Answer

Cite the page or section URL you actually read. If search returns nothing, say so and check `list_docs` rather than inventing a config key, a flag, or a provider id.

Distinguish the published release from what the user is running. `current_release` reports what empryo.com serves. The user's install may be older. When a version difference could change the answer, ask.

## Configure Empryo

Users ask Empryo to set itself up: "use my Claude subscription", "make the cheap model do the
summaries", "turn on computer use", "connect this MCP server", "stop showing me reasoning".

**Use the `settings` tool for this. Do not edit the config JSON by hand.**

`settings` may be available directly or through tool discovery. If hidden, find it with
`tool_search`, inspect it with `run_tool({name: "settings", describe: ""})`, then call it through
`run_tool` with explicit `args`. Use it when a request concerns Empryo's configuration.

| Action | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `settings(action:"list", query:"thinking")` | The writable keys, their types and allowed values. Start here when you are unsure a key exists. |
| `settings(action:"get", key:"diffStyle")` (or `keys:[…]`) | The effective value AND which layer it comes from (project / global / default). |
| `settings(action:"set", key:"thinking.mode", value:"adaptive")` | Write it. `scope` defaults to the layer that already sets the key, else global. |
| `settings(action:"unset", key:"motion")` | Drop the override so the other layer, or Empryo's default, applies again. |

Values arrive as text: `"true"`, `"42"`, and JSON for the array and object keys
(`'["shell"]'`). `null` is only accepted where the key documents it, everywhere else, clearing a
setting is `unset`. The tool refuses a key it does not carry rather than writing a typo nobody
will ever find, so `list` is the check when you are unsure.

Why use the tool instead of editing the JSON file: editing the file by hand changes the file but
not the running app. The desktop app and the terminal UI keep their settings in memory, and only a
change made through the `settings` tool updates them (agents reload, custom providers register,
the Settings panel refreshes). In headless mode there is no UI to update; the tool says so, and the
value applies on the next run.

Most keys apply right away. A few are only read at startup (instruction sources, live
translations, live skills, the Neovim binary and config, LSP auto-install, telemetry). Trust the
tool's reply:

- `Applied live on the <surface> — the UI already shows it.` → say so and stop.
- `… only read at startup, TELL THE USER to restart Empryo (/restart on the terminal, quit and
  reopen the app on desktop).` → the write LANDED, end your answer by asking them to restart. Do
  not restart anything yourself, and do not pretend the change is visible.

`list` marks those keys `[next launch]`. Report what the tool said, never promise more.

The desktop app's look (`appearance.*`: theme, density, opacity) belongs to the desktop app and
can only be changed from a running desktop window. From the terminal or headless, the tool refuses
these keys.

Two files, project wins:

| Scope | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Global | `~/.empryo/config.json` |
| Project | `.empryo/config.json` |

The tool picks the file, and you can override it: `scope: "global"` writes
`~/.empryo/config.json` (every project on this machine), `scope: "project"` writes
`.empryo/config.json` (this repo only, `"local"` is accepted for the same thing). Omit `scope`
and it goes to the layer that already sets that key, else global.

Match the scope to what the user said. A general preference ("I like compact diffs", "always use
my Claude subscription") is global. "For this repo", "here" or "on this project" is project. Never
write a setting the user wanted everywhere to the project file: a project value overrides the
global one for that repo without any visible sign, and other repos will behave differently. The write
clears the same key from the other layer, so the scope you choose is the one in force.

The path is the same every time:

1. Retrieve the setting and confirm it exists in this version, `reference/configuration` is the
   key list, `reference/commands` the slash commands, `reference/cli` the flags. `settings`
   `list` is the fast local check. The docs say what the value MEANS.
2. `settings` `get` first, so you can report what changed and from which layer.
3. Write ONE thing. Say which scope you wrote and why.
4. Report the tool's own line back: it names the before/after value, the scope, and whether the
   running surface already applied it.

Things `settings` does not do on purpose. Use the app's own flow and tell the user:

| Ask | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Sign in to a subscription, add or remove an API key | `/login`, `/keys`, `empryo --set-key`, credentials never go through a config write |
| Connect an MCP server | `mcpServers` in the config file, then `/mcp`, an array of server definitions, not a scalar |
| Custom providers | `providers` in the config file; the repo must be TRUSTED or it is dropped |
| Install an addon, upgrade, change trust | ask first: `/trust`, `/addons`, `empryo upgrade` |

### Where the same settings live in the UI

Tell the user where they could have changed it themselves, so they learn the app.

| Surface | Where |
| --- | --- |
| Desktop | Settings (⌘,), General, Appearance, Models, Provider, Tools, Privacy, Cells. Every row writes the same two files, with a scope selector per row. |
| Terminal | `/settings` for the panel; `/model`, `/theme`, `/effort`, `/thinking`, `/provider`, `/provider-settings`, `/tools`, `/language`, `/mcp`, `/skills`, `/agents`, `/hooks` for one thing each. |
| Headless | `--model`, `--mode`, `--effort`, `--locale`, `--agent`, `--skill`, `--trust` override one run without writing config. |

Commands that show the current state without changing it. Run these before and after a change:

| Ask | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Which providers hold a key | `empryo --list-providers` |
| Which models a provider serves | `empryo --list-models <provider>` |
| What provider tools resolve to on a model | `empryo --capabilities [model]` |
| Whether the runtime is healthy | `empryo doctor` |

### Routing by cost

"Make the cheap model do the summaries" is two tools, in this order:

1. `find_model`, the rows carry the PUBLISHED price in USD per 1M tokens:
   `in $1 / out $5 / cache-r $0.1 / cache-w $1.25`. Search the family or the provider
   ("haiku", "gemini flash", "openrouter"), read the prices, and pick from the rows: it lists
   only providers the user can run now, and names the ones that would need a key when none can.
2. `settings set taskRouter '{"spark":"anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5"}'`, the router MERGES per
   slot, so one call changes one job and leaves the rest of the router alone.

A row with no price means nobody published one, say that instead of guessing, and never
present a rate you did not read from the tool. Prices are list rates: they exclude the user's
discounts, tax, and any subscription seat where tokens are not billed at all.

The slots are in `recipes/task-router`, `empryo --list-models <provider>` is the same catalog
from the shell.

Common requests and where they are documented:

| Request | Page | Keys or commands |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sign in to a subscription or add a key | `providers/subscriptions`, `providers/overview` | `/login`, `/keys`, `empryo --set-key` |
| Change the default model | `reference/configuration` | `defaultModel`, `/model` |
| Different models for different jobs | `recipes/task-router` | `taskRouter` slots |
| Thinking mode, effort, retries | `context/provider-options` | `thinking`, `performance.effort`, `retry` |
| Computer use, code execution, text editor, provider-side search | `context/provider-tools` | `computerUse`, `codeExecution`, `anthropicTextEditor`, `nativeSearch` |
| Connect an MCP server | `tools/mcp` | `mcpServers`, `/mcp` |
| Context window filling up | `context/compaction` | `compaction`, `/compact` |
| Look and feel, transcript, diffs | `tools/themes`, `surfaces/desktop`, `surfaces/tui` | `theme.name`, `diffStyle`, `chatLayout`, `motion` |
| Hooks, skills, agents, memory | one page each under Tools | `/hooks`, `/skills`, `/agents`, `/memory` |
| Desktop panels and boards | `tools/morphs` | `.empryo/morphs`, `/morphs`, `cells.reach` |
| Where a morph appears in the window (a pane, a fixed spot in the app frame, a lane header, the canvas) | `tools/morphs` | `surface.place`, `extensions[].target` (a fixed list of targets), `slot` |
| Untrusted repo dropped my config | `reference/configuration` | `/trust`, `--trust` |

A project checkout that has not been trusted runs without its `mcpServers`, `providers`,
`extraBody` and presets. Check that before diagnosing a setting that "does nothing", and before
writing the same setting a second time.

## Doc map

Every slug below is a page: `https://empryo.com/docs/<slug>.md`, or `read_docs` with that slug.
Search first. This map is for when you already know which page you want.

<!-- docs-index:start — generated by scripts/build-empryo-skill-index.ts, do not edit by hand -->

**Get started** — `index` Introduction · `installation` Installation · `quickstart` Quickstart · `terminal-guide` Terminal lessons · `faq` FAQ · `agents/docs-mcp` Docs for agents
